title: Threshold-Averaged Expected Shortfall Under Weak Identification
content: Peaks-over-threshold estimates of Expected Shortfall (ES) depend on the threshold, and averaging over thresholds is a common remedy. In short samples this remedy is unreliable, and much of the instability can be traced to near-singular shape estimates that occur across the grid, while value-at-risk up to 99.5% is hardly affected. Formally, the ES is then weakly identified: its Fisher information vanishes as the shape approaches one, and its likelihood-ratio confidence set is unbounded whenever the data cannot reject a shape of one. Using 5,700 simulated samples, three fire-insurance portfolios, two equity loss series and six market series, we compare six protections against near-singular estimates with Bayesian threshold averaging and automated threshold selection. The problem depends on sample length and tail weight rather than asset class: unprotected annual insurance estimates reach 5 to 48 times the full-sample value, one-year market windows, raw or GARCH-filtered, show occasional blow-ups that the protections largely remove, and long samples are unaffected. Every protection removes most of the error of an equal-weight average, none is best everywhere, and out-of-sample differences are rarely significant. A bootstrap upper bound on the fitted shape flags weakly identified samples more precisely than the disagreement between estimators.
